body.title: Acoustic Granite: The 56 Resonant Pillars of Vijaya Vittala
body.orientation: How Vijayanagara sculptors cut monolithic granite columns that ring with musical notes, turning stone into sacred sound.

hero.alt: Intricately carved stone pillars of Vijaya Vittala temple hall at Hampi

paragraphs.text: The Vijaya Vittala Temple, begun in the 15th century and expanded during Emperor Krishnadevaraya's reign, houses the famed Ranga Mandapa with 56 musical pillars (SaReGaMa pillars).
Each main pillar is surrounded by seven slender micro-pillars carved out of a single monolithic block of resonant granite that produce distinct bell-like tones when tapped.
Scholars suggest these pillars served as acoustic accompaniment to temple dancers and liturgical chants during sacred nocturnal festivals.
The musical pillars represent the apex of Dravidian stone craftsmanship, proving that medieval artisans understood stone density, sonic vibration, and architectural resonance.

claims.text: The Vittala temple mandapa featuring musical pillars was built during the 15th–16th centuries of Vijayanagara rule.

evidence.excerpt: The Vijaya Vittala temple dates to the 15th century, with substantial additions made by King Krishnadevaraya in the 16th century.

claims.text: Clusters of slender colonnettes carved from a single granite block emit musical pitches.

evidence.excerpt: The pillars are carved out of single pieces of granite; when struck gently, each colonnette produces a clear musical note.

claims.text: Acoustic resonance supported liturgical dance and musical ceremonies in the Ranga Mandapa.

evidence.excerpt: Tradition holds that the pillars provided acoustic accompaniment to religious dances and temple celebrations.

claims.text: The pillars demonstrate advanced metallurgical and mineralogical knowledge of granite resonance.

evidence.excerpt: Studies note varying mineral compositions and densities in the granite chosen specifically for acoustic performance.
